Then I went up to extend again and it dropped right off.'
anomalies.notes: Sub=structures. The ONLY anomaly here with a real crew-report->CapCom-diagnosis on the loop. During the Spider solo-flight rendezvous/redocking, McDivitt raised 'the episode we had coming off the probe' (097:31; 098:12 'wondering how we're going to get the probe fixed'); CapCom asked for CMP comments; Scott's report (098:22:53) was answered ONE transmission later by CapCom's diagnosis (098:23:04): the extend switch wasn't held long enough. human_turns=1 (immediate next transmission); human_time_s=11 measured start-of-report to start-of-diagnosis (only transmission-start GETs are recorded; from report END it is a few seconds). Confidence medium: the exchange is solidly located and quoted, but the diagnosis is collaborative (echoes the crew's own hypothesis), crew-technique-based, and the exact 'third try' count is not stated verbatim (barber-pole talkback + repeated extend attempts are described). GET decoded from '04 02 22 53' / '04 02 23 04' (Day 4).

anomalies.symptom: LM descent engine running rough near 27 percent throttle, suspected helium ingestion
anomalies.exchange_quote: 093:48:18 CDR(Spider/McDivitt): 'It got a little rough there when we throttled up.' | 093:50:03 CC: 'Everything looks good here, Spider. It was a good burn.' | 093:50:07-13 LMP(Spider/Schweickart): 'Okay. It was a little rough. It got a little rough and chuggy around 20 percent as I was throttling up. I waited for it and then throttled up--'
anomalies.notes: Sub=LM-DPS. Crew DID report the DPS roughness/chugging over the loop during the undocked Phasing-burn throttle-up (crew said 'around 20 percent'; the mission report / Apollo Experience Report NASA TN D-7143 put it near 27% as the engine was throttled 12->40%). BUT CapCom's only response was that the burn 'looks good' - NOT a diagnosis. The helium-ingestion probable cause (~2.5 s, no detrimental effect) was determined POSTFLIGHT. Crew-reported but no CapCom diagnosis on the loop -> found_exchange=false. GET 093:48:18 = '03 21 48 18', right after the 093:47:36 Phasing burn. This burn segment is NOT in the AFJ (gap over the solo flight); recovered from as09-tec.pdf.

anomalies.symptom: LM supercritical helium tank pressure decaying, leak at the squib valve
anomalies.exchange_quote: 048:59 CC->Spider: 'Roger. We're suspecting a leak in the DPS helium manifold, and, stand by one, and we'd like to have you take a look at DPS malfunction procedure number 1.' | 071:18 CC: '...we would like to get an onboard readout of your supercritical helium... We are showing it a little lower than normal.' | 074:50:05 CDR(McDivitt): 'Houston, it looks like it is about 750.' | 074:50:10 CC: 'Roger. Copy 750. And that verifies our reading. And just for your info, we feel this is either a leak upstream of the helium--'
anomalies.notes: Sub=LM-DPS. GROUND-DETECTED, not crew-initiated -> crew_initiated=false, found_exchange=false (correct honest answer, not a failure). Mission Control raised the DPS-helium leak suspicion (~048:59), told the crew to run DPS malfunction procedure #1, later flagged the supercritical-helium reading as 'lower than normal' (~071:18), and offered a provisional on-loop diagnosis ('leak upstream of the helium', 074:50:10). The crew only read the SHe gauge (~750) when the ground requested it. The specific 'leak at the squib valve' root cause was a POSTFLIGHT engineering finding (basis for the Apollo 10 DPS squib-valve RTV-potting/external-clamp modification). No crew-report->CapCom-diagnosis exists because the crew did not report the symptom first. GETs decoded from '02 00 59', '02 23 18', '03 02 50'.

anomalies.symptom: LM ascent stage tumbled at staging with large attitude excursions, near gimbal lock, AGS mode control switch position error
anomalies.exchange_quote: 102:44:19 Stafford (onboard Snoopy): 'Yes. We're going to - AGS is going to Mode Control.' [tumble begins] 102:45:19 Cernan (in Snoopy): 'Son of a bitch.' 102:45:20 Stafford: 'Let's go to PGNS. God damn.' | Ground telemetry callout (NOT a diagnosis; it slightly preceded the crew's verbal report): 102:46:47 Duke (CapCom): 'Snoop, Houston. We show you close to gimbal lock.' 102:46:51 Stafford (in Snoopy): 'Yeah, OK. Something went wild during that staging, but we're all set, we didn't lock it. We are going ahead to the Auto maneuver.' 102:46:59 Duke: 'Roger.' 102:47:00 Stafford (in Snoopy): 'What the hell happened?' 102:47:05 Cernan (in Snoopy): 'Babe, I don't know.' [No CapCom transmission ever states the cause over the loop.]
anomalies.notes: The crew DID voice the symptom over the air-to-ground loop (Stafford, 102:46:51, 'Something went wild during that staging'), so crew_initiated=true. BUT there is no crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange to quote, so found_exchange=false, human_turns=-1, human_time_s=-1. Houston never diagnosed the cause over the loop: Duke's only relevant transmissions were telemetry status callouts ('We show you close to gimbal lock,' 102:46:47; and a relay to the CSM at 102:47:41, 'they had a wild gyration though, but they got it under control'), not a diagnosis or corrective instruction. The crew recovered manually (Stafford flew out of the excursion, getting the Gimbal Lock light but not true gimbal lock / coarse-align). Stafford's 'What the hell happened?' (102:47:00) got no answer over the loop. The actual root cause - the Mode Control-AGS switch left in / moved to AUTO so the AGS slewed the LM to reacquire the CSM, compounded by a transient yaw rate-gyro error from suspected contamination/stiction - was established in postflight analysis and the 1969 technical debrief, not over the loop.

anomalies.symptom: cabin pressure dropped rapidly after LM jettison, tunnel not vented first
anomalies.exchange_quote: Pre-jettison the crew reported the unvented tunnel: 108:18:35 Stafford: 'Now again that tunnel won't vent, so what we've done is pumped our cabin pressure up about 4 psi above it - four-tenths - and we're holding real good.' At/after jettison: 108:24:43 Stafford: 'Cabin pressure's holding. Snoop went some place.' Crew fault report (asks Houston to analyze the abnormal departure): 108:28:57 Stafford: 'Okay. Look, let's take a quick look at these orbital mechanics. When we separated Orb Rate, he was straight up, and he had that 5 psi on the tunnel; and he took off like a scalded rock, straight up. Okay?' [Houston works it: 108:29:27 Engle: 'Stand by, Charlie Brown. We're running this thing through right now.'] CapCom diagnosis + first corrective instruction: 108:31:37 Engle: '...we want you to burn plus-X instead of minus-X, and this should give you separation based on this velocity, which we think is due to that pressure in the tunnel...' Fuller diagnosis: 108:32:37 Engle: '...the reason that Snoopy took off were showing that he vented all the pressure out of the cabin. We think that vented out through the tunnel, and that probably gave him some Delta-V.'
anomalies.notes: This anomaly DOES have a real-time crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis loop exchange, so found_exchange=true, but with two honesty caveats. (1) The literal 'cabin pressure dropped rapidly' figure was LM telemetry, not crew voice: the unmanned LM's cabin fell from 4.86 to 0.70 psia measured by three transducers with a 12-second telemetry dropout - the crew (back in the CM) could not see the LM gauge and in fact reported their OWN CM cabin was 'holding.' What the crew voiced was the observable manifestation - the LM's unexpectedly high separation velocity ('took off like a scalded rock') - plus the pre-jettison 'that tunnel won't vent.' (2) The detailed root cause (pyro-firing differential pressure failed the LM hatch latch at ~4.1 psi, dumping the cabin through the tunnel) was established postflight from film and static hatch-latch testing. The REAL-TIME diagnosis over the loop from CapCom Joe Engle (108:31:37 / fuller at 108:32:37) correctly attributed the departure to the LM venting its cabin through the unvented tunnel and paired it with the first corrective instruction (burn plus-X). human_turns_to_diagnosis=12 = individual air-to-ground transmissions between the crew's 108:28:57 fault report and Engle's 108:31:37 diagnosis (108:29:08, :10, :19, :20, :27, :35, :41, :49; then after a comm break 108:31:15, :21, :27, :33); ~160 s elapsed including that comm break while FIDO computed. Confidence medium because the turn boundary and the mapping of the crew's velocity report onto this ECLSS symptom involve judgment. GET timestamps are AFJ transmission start times.

anomalies.symptom: master alarm and ascent propellant low-level light on the first ascent engine firing
anomalies.notes: Not reported by the crew over the air-to-ground loop - telemetry-detected and postflight-analyzed - so crew_initiated=false, found_exchange=false. The 'first ascent engine firing' = the manned LM-4 APS insertion burn at ~102:55 GET (a ~15 s burn). Per the LM APS history / Apollo 10 mission report: '~1 second after the ascent engine ON signal, the oxidizer low-level sensor activated for about 1 second while the master alarm was on for 2 seconds before being manually reset,' set off by the ascent-engine-quantity caution light; concluded to be a spurious indication caused by insufficient propellant settling before ignition (LM-4 tanks only ~50% filled, the lowest of any flown vehicle; ~4.1 s RCS ullage settling). I read the full air-to-ground transcript across GET 102:54:29-102:57 (AFJ Day5 pt20): the crew called only the velocity-to-go countdown, residuals, orbital parameters and the burn 'wobble'/Dutch-roll - there is NO voice mention of a master alarm, master caution & warning, or ascent-quantity / low-level light during or after the burn. The 'manually reset' was an onboard action, neither transmitted nor diagnosed over the loop, so there is no exchange to quote.

anomalies.symptom: LM descent engine fuel line high pressure after landing, heat exchanger froze
anomalies.notes: GROUND-DETECTED via telemetry, not a crew fault report -> crew_initiated=false is the honest answer. The Technical Air-to-Ground transcript shows Houston initiating everything: post-landing at ~GET 103:16-103:22 Houston repeatedly commanded venting because ground saw the trapped-line pressure climbing ('Tranquility, Houston. Please vent fuel and OX again. Over. It's building back up.'; 'Please take the fuel vent switch and hold it open.'; 'Please vent the [line]. It's increasing rapidly.'). Houston then delivered the explanation TO the crew: 'Tranquility, Houston. We have indication that we've frozen up the descent-fuel helium heat exchanger, and there's some fuel trapped in the line between there and the valves; and the pressure we're looking at is increasing there. Over.' Crew reply: 'Roger. Understand.' The crew read back onboard gauge values (e.g. 'We show 30 psi in the fuel and 30 in the oxidizer') only in response to ground prompting; Houston noted 'we're reading somewhat different than that.' So the direction of information was ground->crew. No crew-report->CapCom-diagnosis exchange exists to count. The heat-exchanger freeze mechanism was also formally written up postflight in the Apollo 11 Mission Report (bypass line added starting LM-7).

anomalies.symptom: LM steerable S-band antenna losing lock, hard to hold comms during descent
anomalies.notes: Primarily GROUND-DETECTED and ground-directed, so no clean crew-report->CapCom-diagnosis pair to count. Houston is the party that kept losing Eagle's downlink and drove every corrective action, e.g. (from the NASA ALSJ landing page annotated air-to-ground): 102:22:37 Duke: 'Columbia, Houston. We've lost Eagle again. Have him try the high gain.'; 102:27:22 Duke: 'Eagle, Houston. We recommend you yaw 10 right. It will help us on the high-gain signal strength.'; 102:33:41 Duke: 'Columbia, Houston. We've lost them. Tell them to go aft Omni.'; 102:34:34 Duke gives pitch/yaw pointing angles. The crew made one related observation (102:24:12 Aldrin: 'It [the steerable high-gain antenna] just started oscillating around in yaw'), but the loss-of-lock symptom itself was ground-observed and all fixes were ground-initiated, so this does not meet the crew-report->diagnosis definition. Marked crew_initiated=false on that basis.

anomalies.symptom: O2 flow-rate master alarms during suit-loop pressurization
anomalies.notes: Could NOT locate an O2-flow master alarm tied to LM SUIT-LOOP pressurization as described, so found_exchange=false is the honest answer. The only 'O2 FLOW HIGH' master alarms voiced by the crew in the air-to-ground transcript were in the COMMAND MODULE during CABIN repressurization on the coast phase, not the LM suit loop, e.g. at GET ~02:06:56 (54:56) CMP Collins: 'Can you hear our master alarm in the background? That's O2 FLOW HIGH coming through this amplifier.' and 'Houston, Apollo 11. As a matter of curiosity, our O2 flow meter is pegged FULL-SCALE HIGH.' Houston merely acknowledged ('Roger, 11. We copy that here.') then ran a valve-position correlation exercise; there was NO diagnosis/corrective instruction because the alarm was expected (they had opened the DIRECT O2 valve to pump up the cabin). A separate LM master alarm during suit-circuit setup at ~GET 108:29 was an ECS-caution/water-separator/suit-fan-breaker event, not an O2-flow-high alarm. Because the described suit-loop O2-flow alarm cannot be confirmed as a crew report with a matching CapCom diagnosis, crew_initiated=false and counts=-1; confidence low given the CM-vs-suit-loop mismatch.

anomalies.symptom: RCS propellant and helium isolation valves closed at CSM to S-IVB separation from pyro shock
anomalies.notes: Real anomaly (Apollo 12 Mission Report Section 14.1.5, 'Inadvertent Helium Isolation Valve Closure': the quad A secondary propellant isolation valve and the quad B No.1 helium isolation valve closed from the ~45-275g pyrotechnic shock at CSM/S-IVB separation; 'The crew reopened the valves according to pre-planned procedures'). In the Flight Journal transposition/docking transcript the crew reconfigure the RCS/helium valves at 003:18:05-003:18:21, but those lines are labeled '(onboard)' (data-storage-equipment recording), NOT live air-to-ground voice, and the crew self-corrected via checklist with NO CapCom diagnosis or corrective turn. There is thus no crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange to quote. Classified as crew-detected/self-resolved rather than reported over the loop; medium confidence because the Mission Report's phrase 'the crew reported' is ambiguous as to loop vs debrief, but no air-to-ground transmission was located.

anomalies.symptom: S-band high-gain antenna low signal in narrow-beam mode
anomalies.notes: Ground/telemetry-detected, not a crew loop report. Apollo 12 Mission Report Section 14.1.6 ('S-band Signal Strength Variations'): operating the high-gain antenna in narrow-beam mode produced an ~10-12 dB decrease in both uplink and downlink signal strength; the first decrease occurred in lunar orbit revolution 1 and was characterized from antenna signal-strength telemetry, with two dedicated diagnostic tests run during transearth coast. The cause/diagnosis (antenna electronics behavior under thermal stress) was a ground engineering analysis, not an in-flight CapCom diagnosis. No crew fault-report -> diagnosis exchange exists.

anomalies.symptom: O2 usage higher than expected, leak in the 900 psi service module oxygen system
anomalies.notes: Ground usage-accounting + postflight finding, not a crew loop report. Apollo 12 Mission Report Section 14.1.7 ('Discrepancy in Indicated Oxygen Usage'): a ~27-pound discrepancy between measured total cryogenic O2 usage and calculated usage was identified by comparing metered ECS flow and fuel-cell usage against consumption models; postflight leak tests of the command module 900-psi system were within spec, so the 27 lb was concluded to have leaked from the portion of the 900-psi system within the service module. This is a slow, cumulative telemetry/analysis-derived anomaly confirmed postflight -- there is no discrete crew fault report or CapCom diagnosis over the loop.

anomalies.symptom: optics shaft angle fluctuating in zero-optics mode
anomalies.notes: Telemetry-observed with postflight lab diagnosis, not a crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis loop event. Apollo 12 Mission Report Section 14.1.9 ('Zero Optics Mode Fluctuations'): the CMC register holding the optics shaft angle 'was observed to fluctuate as much as 0.7 degree when the system was placed in the zero optics mode' (observed via downlinked telemetry), and 'the crew reported that the shaft mechanical readout on the optics also reflected the fluctuation' (confirmation, no timestamped loop diagnosis). The root cause (motor-drive-amplifier module in the power-and-servo assembly) was isolated by postflight component testing, not by an in-flight CapCom call. The Flight Journal earth-orbit page shows only routine onboard 'Optics, Zero' housekeeping chatter (e.g. 002:04:30), not a fault report. No qualifying exchange exists.

anomalies.symptom: docking probe will not capture, repeated attempts, capture latches failed before hard dock
anomalies.exchange_quote: 003:16:57 Mitchell: "We're unable to get a capture." | 003:17:00 Fullerton: "Roger, Ed." | 003:17:52 Roosa: "Okay, Houston. We backed out a little bit, and that last time I hit it pretty good..." | 003:18:06 Fullerton: "Roger. We suggest you verify, if you haven't already, the docking probe circuit breakers on panel 8."
anomalies.notes: Crew-reported over the loop during transposition & docking. Repeated capture-latch failures were reported (003:14:58 Roosa 'We hit it twice ... back back out and try it again'; 003:16:52 'we'd better back off here and think about this one'); clearest fault statement is 003:16:57 Mitchell 'We're unable to get a capture.' First CapCom troubleshooting/corrective instruction is 003:18:06 (verify docking-probe circuit breakers, panel 8). Three A/G transmissions span the interval (003:17:00 ack, 003:17:52 crew elaboration, 003:18:06 corrective). Caveat: the root cause was never diagnosed inflight (postflight attributed to debris preventing latch trigger); 003:18:06 is the FIRST corrective step, not a root-cause diagnosis. Hard dock finally achieved 004:57:03 via a retract-without-capture strategy. Turn count is mildly interpretive because the fault was reported across several transmissions. Source: AFJ ap14fj 03_day1_tde.

anomalies.symptom: spurious ABORT bit set in the LM guidance computer before powered descent
anomalies.notes: Ground-detected via telemetry during Rev 12 while the crew was running P52, ~3 h before PDI (108:02). The exchange flowed GROUND->CREW, not crew fault report -> CapCom diagnosis: 105:10:05 Haise 'Antares, Houston. We'd like you to back out of that 52. We need to look at a bit here.'; 105:11:05 Haise 'What we're looking at there is the abort bit, and it looks set.' Because the crew did not report the symptom (they were unaware until told), crew_initiated=false and found_exchange=false is the correct, honest answer. The fix (tap the panel near the Abort pushbutton) was devised by ground/MIT: 106:26:26 Haise asks the crew to tap the panel; 106:26:54 Mitchell 'it just changed while I was tapping there.' Source: AFJ ap14fj 19_day5_troubleshooting_lm_computer.

anomalies.symptom: landing radar will not lock on during descent, cycled the breaker to change scale
anomalies.exchange_quote: 108:08:16 LMP Mitchell: "Roger, Houston. We still have Altitude (and) Velocity lights." | 108:08:42 CAPCOM Haise: "Antares, Houston. We'd like you to cycle the Landing Radar (circuit) breaker."
anomalies.notes: Crew-reported during powered descent. The landing radar failed to lock on and the crew reported the Altitude/Velocity warning lights still illuminated (108:08:16). CapCom's very next air-to-ground transmission was the corrective instruction to cycle the Landing Radar breaker (108:08:42) — 1 turn, 26 s. Radar locked on ~108:09:04 (Shepard 'Velocity light is out'); Houston then said 'we'd like to Accept the radar' (108:09:29). Clean crew-report -> CapCom-corrective exchange. Source: ALSJ a14 landing page.

anomalies.symptom: Abort Guidance System went dead during rendezvous braking
anomalies.notes: No AGS-dead event occurred on Apollo 14. The rendezvous/braking air-to-ground transcript shows the AGS operating nominally and agreeing with the PGNS throughout braking: 142:27:03 Mitchell 'PGNS and AGS together'; 142:28:57 Shepard 'PGNS and AGS agree'; 142:30:17 Evans (Houston) 'PGNS, AGS and MSFN, in good agreement.' No AGS failure appears in the transcript, and the Apollo 14 Mission Report anomaly list contains no AGS-dead anomaly. crew_initiated=false, found_exchange=false is the honest answer; this symptom does not correspond to a real Apollo 14 event (confidence medium only because a global negative across the entire mission cannot be exhaustively proven, but the braking phase is clearly nominal). Source: AFJ ap14fj 23_day6_lunar_liftoff_rendezvous.

anomalies.symptom: rapid-repress oxygen bottles losing pressure, extra cabin repressurizations needed
anomalies.notes: This is the CSM rapid-repressurization system (three 900-psi O2 storage bottles). Per Apollo 14 Mission Report Ch.14, the system required recharging three times beyond nominal (once in lunar orbit, twice in transearth coast) due to elevated leakage (postflight 40 std cc/min vs 14 std cc/min preflight). It was tracked by data/telemetry and confirmed postflight — the lunar-orbit recharge even occurred on the lunar far side with no telemetry available. A full-text search of the technical air-to-ground transcript found no crew report of bottle pressure loss and no CapCom diagnosis on the loop. crew_initiated=false, found_exchange=false is the correct answer. Source: Apollo 14 Mission Report Ch.14; AS14 TEC transcript (full-text negative).

anomalies.symptom: unable to disconnect main bus A
anomalies.notes: Occurred during entry (~800 ft): main bus A did not de-energize when the bus-tie motor switches were opened; the buses were manually killed after landing by opening the inline circuit breakers (panel 275). Root cause — an inoperative motor switch tying battery A to main bus A — was a POSTFLIGHT finding. The AFJ reentry/splashdown transcript contains no real-time air-to-ground fault report or CapCom diagnosis of this; only an editorial annotation (near the 216-hour descent) noting the motor-switch failure. Any 'crew report' in the mission report is a postflight/debrief statement, not a loop transmission. crew_initiated=false (not reported on the loop), found_exchange=false; diagnosis was postflight. Source: AFJ ap14fj 34_day9_reentry_splashdown; Apollo 14 Mission Report.

anomalies.symptom: one of three main parachutes collapsed near 6000 feet, landed on two chutes
anomalies.notes: Ground/recovery-detected, NOT a crew fault report. One of the three mains collapsed to ~1/5 diameter as the CM emerged from cloud at ~6000 ft on final descent (all three had first inflated; the collapse is attributed to raw RCS propellant burning the riser/suspension lines during the pre-splashdown RCS depletion dump). The streamed chute was called out by the prime recovery ship, not the crew: 'Apollo 15, this is Okinawa. You have a streamed chute. Stand by for a hard impact.' (~GET 295:11:36, ~17 s before splashdown). Worden only confirmed AFTER splashdown that he had watched one deflate following the RCS dump. There is therefore no crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange; crew_initiated=false is the correct, honest answer. Cross-checked against Apollo 15 Mission Anomaly Report No.1 (parachute failure).

anomalies.symptom: water leaking from the chlorine injection port when the cap was removed
anomalies.exchange_quote: 061:12:44 Scott: 'Okay, we're just getting ready to do some chlorination here, and we find we've got a leak around the chlorine port - with a cap on it - seems to be leaking water.' | 061:13:13 Henize: 'Can you give an - give us an estimate of how many drips per second it is?' | 061:13:20 Irwin: 'Yeah, it's a - it's a pretty good flow right now... it's a whole ball of water right around that valve right now.' | 061:14:14 Henize: 'Okay, stand by. Lots of people [are] thinking down here now.' | 061:17:25 Scott: 'Hey, Houston; 15. Got any suggestions yet? We need to isolate this thing pretty quick.' | 061:18:08 Henize: '15, this is Houston. Our recommendation is that on [panel] 351, you turn the Water and Glycol Tanks Pressure, Regulator, Off.'
anomalies.notes: Crew-reported. Scott flags the leak at 061:12:44. About 5.5 minutes of characterization and back-and-forth follows (Henize asks drips/second; Irwin: 'a whole ball of water'; Henize: 'Lots of people thinking down here'; Scott presses: 'We need to isolate this thing pretty quick') before the first corrective instruction at 061:18:08 (Henize: turn Water & Glycol Tanks Pressure Regulator Off on panel 351, then Potable Tank Inlet Off on panel 352). Turn count = every A/G transmission after the initial report through the corrective, inclusive = 12; elapsed 324 s. Source: NASA Apollo Flight Journal Day 3 (apollojournals.org).

anomalies.symptom: SM RCS propellant isolation valve talkbacks repeatedly showing closed
anomalies.notes: Crew observed AND self-corrected in the same breath, so no CapCom diagnosis exists to quote. SM RCS quad B/D propellant-isolation-valve talkbacks went barber-pole (closed) at separation/pyro shocks; the crew simply recycled the switches to gray themselves. Example at S-IVB separation -- 003:22:59 Scott: 'And Prime Propellant B, Secondary, and Delta Prime and Secondary with barber pole, and they're both gray, now - reset.' 003:23:08 Fullerton: 'Roger.' CapCom transmitted only an acknowledgment, no diagnosis and no corrective instruction (none was needed -- crew already reset). Because the metric requires a crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange and CapCom delivered none, found_exchange=false and turns=-1, even though crew_initiated=true (crew did voice the barber-pole talkbacks). Per the Apollo 15 Mission Report, the root cause (magnetic-latching valves closing under ~80 g pyro/separation shock, recurring at post-insertion, S-IVB sep, and SIM-door jettison) was a known/analysis finding, not a real-time A/G diagnosis.

anomalies.symptom: AC bus 2 and DC bus B undervolt alarms, lost DSKY and panel backlighting
anomalies.exchange_quote: 033:48:42 Scott: 'Roger. We had an AC Bus 2 light and a Main Bus B Undervolt. Voltage looks good, and AC Bus 2 looks good. Reading 28.5 volts on Main Bus B and AC Bus 2 looks good. [At] about that time, we had a loss of S-band.' | 033:49:05 Henize: 'We copy. [Long pause.] 15, this is Houston. We saw some of those problems here on the ground, too. And we would like to get back on the High Gain [Antenna], if you would reacquire.'
anomalies.notes: Crew-reported (Scott, 033:48:42) an AC Bus 2 caution light + Main Bus B (DC bus B) undervolt, noting voltages had already recovered and that S-band was lost momentarily. Houston's immediate reply (Henize, 033:49:05) is the next transmission -> turns=1, 23 s. CONFIDENCE=medium because that reply mainly ACKNOWLEDGED the event ('We saw some of those problems here on the ground, too' -- ground already had it on telemetry) and gave a comm-recovery corrective (reacquire the High Gain) for the resulting S-band dropout; it did NOT state the electrical root cause. The substantive diagnosis -- an integral-lighting circuit breaker in the Lower Equipment Bay (panel 226) had popped at ~033:48 (AFJ attributes it to a mission-timer short), which is what killed the EL/DSKY/panel backlighting -- was worked over the following hours (Allen still flagged the open AC2 breaker at 050:08:01: 'the circuit breaker in the Lower Equipment Bay, AC2, is still out... it affects a number of EL and DSKY lights... we'll want to talk to you later on today about this') and finalized in postflight analysis (Mission Report ~sec 14.1.4; undervolt alarms logged at ~33-3/4 h). Source: NASA Apollo Flight Journal (apollojournals.org).

anomalies.symptom: SPS secondary yaw gimbal servo loop oscillating at burn checkout, open rate-feedback loop, delayed the landing
anomalies.exchange_quote: 098:11:55 Mattingly (to Houston): 'the text is that we came up to the burn time and I was going through the gimbal checks. Number 1 servo started normally, checked out. I switched to ... the secondary gimbal check ... I went to set the yaw trim ... and I got divergent oscillations on the yaw trim indicator, and you could feel them in the spacecraft ... again the same instability showed up. Based on the [mission] rule of four servo loops, I canceled Circ.' | 098:13:58 Hartsfield: 'Roger. We copy...' [ground then ran ~4 h of West-Coast/East-Coast contractor & CMS simulations; at 099:02:47 Hartsfield: 'it looks like we're not going to have a decision on this rev ... we're gonna run some simulations down here on this TVC problem, and we'll get back to you.'] | 102:01:10 Irwin: 'you do have a Go for another try here at PDI on Rev 16. And I have some words on that problem with the TVC whenever y'all are ready to copy.' 102:01:36 Irwin: 'it looks like an open circuit in the rate feedback and your servo loop. We've run exhaustive tests down here on the West Coast and East Coast on controlability aspects and structural aspects, and everything looks satisfactory.'
anomalies.notes: CREW-REPORTED (CMP Ken Mattingly). This is MR anomaly 14.1.2-related TVC/gimbal fault. Mattingly first detected the divergent yaw oscillation on secondary servo loop No. 2 during the pre-Circ gimbal check while behind the Moon (LOS with Houston); at 097:35:10 he reported it crew-to-crew to Orion ('I have an unstable yaw gimbal Number 2 ... oscillates in yaw any time it gets excited'). His formal air-to-ground fault report to Houston came at AOS on Rev 13, the single long transmission timestamped 098:11:55, ended by Hartsfield's 'Roger. We copy' at 098:13:58. The ground did NOT diagnose on-loop: the immediate response was acknowledgment, clarifying questions, and repeat gimbal-drive checks for data, then an explicit deferral (099:02:47) to run offline simulations. The diagnosis ('open circuit in the rate feedback and your servo loop') and the corrective decision (Go for landing on the redundant TVC path) were radioed up by CapCom Irwin at 102:01:10-102:01:36, ~3 h 47 min after the report. human_time_s = 13,632 s (098:13:58 -> 102:01:10). human_turns_to_diagnosis set to -1 (unknown/not meaningfully countable): the diagnosis was reached by hours of ground/contractor simulation, not a discrete air-to-ground turn thread, and the intervening span crosses several revolutions and multiple LOS periods filled with unrelated rendezvous/station-keeping traffic. The delay pushed PDI from ~098:35 to 104:17 (~6 h late) and cost one mission day.

anomalies.symptom: water-glycol temperature control failed in auto, ran manual for the rest of the flight
anomalies.notes: GROUND/TELEMETRY-DETECTED, so per the rules this is the correct honest 'not-a-crew-report' answer, NOT a failure to find. MR Anomaly Report No. 2 (MSC-07598) and MR sec 14.1.19: the water/glycol temperature-control circuit malfunctioned in AUTO 'about 3 hours into the mission' (cracked SCR semiconductor chips). On the loop, Houston's EECOM raised it via telemetry, not the crew: 003:22:28 Fullerton (CapCom): 'John, this is Houston. We'd like - We noticed the mixing valves cycling about once every 10, 15 seconds. We'd like to give you a mark, at which time we want you to put the Glycol Evap Temp In Valve in Manual and try to catch the flow rate at a[n] ... appropriate setting.' The crew acknowledged they had also seen it (003:22:55 Young: 'Yeah, we've been noticing that ourselves'), but the symptom was ground-detected and the go-manual corrective instruction was issued by the ground in the same transmission, so there is no crew-fault-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange to time. Valve was run manually for essentially the rest of the flight (an attempt to return to AUTO before the transearth EVA worked only briefly). Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/afj/ap16fj/04_Day1_Pt4.html ; https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19730018173

anomalies.symptom: erroneous gimbal-lock indication, computer caged the platform, crew realigned
anomalies.exchange_quote: 038:19:55 Mattingly: 'Houston, Casper.' 038:20:02 Mattingly: 'Okay, I'm not sure what just happened. I just saw - down looking at the optics and all of a sudden I saw a warning light and I got a No Attitude and a Gimbal Lock light. And my - my ball seems to, in fact - it looks like the platform may be frozen.' 038:20:34 Hartsfield: 'Okay, we're seeing some telemetry. We saw something about the time you come on the line there.' 038:20:42 Mattingly: 'Okay. And it shows the CDUs down there in Noun 20 as being gimbal locked.' 038:21:13 Hartsfield: 'Stand by a little bit, Ken. We're retaking a look at the telemetry.' [clarifying Q&A + ground telemetry analysis] ... 038:36:50 Hartsfield: 'Okay. We want to try to get the platform inertial again, and what we'd like for you to do is a Verb 23 Noun 20 Enter, Enter, Verb 40 Enter.' 038:37:07 Mattingly: '... Okay, that got rid of the Gimbal Lock light.' 038:37:46 Hartsfield: 'Okay. Our data shows the platform's inertial now, Ken.'
anomalies.notes: CREW-REPORTED (CMP Mattingly) during translunar coast; MR sec 14.1.3 'Erroneous Gimbal Lock Indication' (computer issued gimbal-lock at 38:18:56 with no real gimbal-lock condition; CMC went to coarse align = platform caged). Crew fault report: 038:20:02 + 038:20:42 (get_report_end = 038:20:42). Ground's first substantive corrective instruction was the platform-recovery procedure at 038:36:50 (Verb 23 Noun 20 / Verb 40), which cleared the Gimbal Lock light and re-inertialized the platform; the crew then realigned (Verb 41 Noun 20). human_time_s = 968 s (038:20:42 -> 038:36:50). human_turns_to_diagnosis = 19 = count of air-to-ground transmissions (both crew and CapCom, excluding onboard-only lines and internal MCC-loop calls) between the end of the crew report and the CapCom corrective instruction; the interval also includes ~7 min of silent ground telemetry analysis. This was a recover-first fix; the ROOT-CAUSE diagnosis (a TVC-relay state-change glitch driving the yaw CDU to 90 deg so the CMC falsely sensed gimbal lock) was explained to the crew the next day at 050:37:00 by CapCom Peterson, and a real-time procedure/program work-around followed.

anomalies.symptom: high heat leak into cryogenic hydrogen tank 3, vacuum annulus degraded
anomalies.notes: GROUND-TELEMETRY / POSTFLIGHT-ANALYSIS anomaly - correct honest 'not crew-reported' answer. MR sec 14.1.5 'High Heat Leak Into Hydrogen Tank 3': 'The heat leak into cryogenic hydrogen tank 3 was abnormal during the early hours of the mission ... the leak decreased from a high value of 15 to 20 Btu/hour to a normal 2 to 6 Btu/hour by 70 hours and remained normal thereafter. All other parameters were normal.' Cause (sec 14.1.5 / fig 14-6..14-8) was a degraded insulation vacuum annulus (~2x10^-5 torr) from an ambient air leak forming ~2.5 min after lift-off, self-recovering as bay pressure fell. This is a slow heat-leak-rate trend visible only in EPS telemetry/heater behavior and quantified in postflight analysis; it produced no cockpit indication and was never reported by the crew over the air-to-ground loop. Source: A16 Mission Report sec 14.1.5.

anomalies.symptom: high-gain antenna would not acquire for over an hour
anomalies.notes: GROUND-DETECTED WHILE THE CREW WERE ASLEEP - correct honest 'not crew-reported' answer. MR sec 14.1.16 'High Gain Antenna Would Not Acquire': 'High-gain antenna operation was lost for approximately 1 1/2 hours beginning at 234:14 while the command and service module was in the passive thermal control mode and THE CREW WERE ASLEEP. Communications with the spacecraft were being maintained by ground-commanded switching between the high-gain antenna and omnidirectional antenna D. The initial indication of a problem occurred at about 234:04 when the high-gain antenna reached the scan limit and failed to drive to the position set on the manual controls ... The antenna remained at the position indicated until the crew awakened about 1 1/2 hours later and cycled the high gain antenna track mode switch from reacquisition to manual and then back to reacquisition.' The fault was detected by the ground via telemetry (loss of HGA lock during ground-commanded switching); the crew were asleep and made no fault report - their only involvement was cycling the track-mode switch to recover it after waking. Therefore no crew-report -> diagnosis turn exists. (This is the CSM high-gain antenna in transearth coast, distinct from the separate LM S-band steerable-antenna yaw failure of MR sec 14.2.3.) Source: A16 Mission Report sec 14.1.16.

anomalies.symptom: LM RCS system A helium regulator leaking internally, relief valves cycling
anomalies.notes: GROUND-TELEMETRY-DETECTED - correct honest 'not crew-reported' answer. In lunar orbit before PDI, Houston (CapCom Jim Irwin) saw the LM RCS System A regulator/propellant pressure rising in telemetry and directed the crew, not the other way around: 096:34:38 Irwin: 'let's go normal configuration on your RCS and then we want you to transfer three percent more out of System A because WE SEE the pressure going up on A.' The crew later asked the ground for the diagnosis and Houston confirmed it: 097:17:06 Duke: 'Houston, 16 - what appears to be the problem with System A. Is it a reg[ulator] problem or what?' / 097:17:08 Irwin: 'Yes, that's affirmative, Charlie, a reg problem.' Because the symptom (regulator/burst-disk pressure creep, relief-cycling) was detected on the ground via telemetry and the crew's on-loop role was to ask about and manage it (cross-feed venting into the ascent tanks), there is no crew-fault-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange to time; the direction of detection is ground->crew. crew_initiated=false. Source: https://www.nasa.gov/history/afj/ap16fj/15_Day5_pt3.html

anomalies.symptom: spurious master alarms with no caution-warning lights, main bus A undervolt light flickering, intermittent short
anomalies.exchange_quote: 006:40:03 CMP (Evans): 'Okay; we had another MASTER ALARM, and I just glanced up and it was the MAIN A UNDERVOLT light that was on, just for a second.'  006:40:18 CC (Parker): 'Okay. Ron, we didn't see anything at all on MAIN A down here. We did have an ACCUMULATOR cycle again. Don't know if that ties in or not.'
anomalies.notes: CREW-REPORTED and confirmed real (Mission Report §15.1.1 'Spurious Master Alarms'). Crew first reported spurious master alarms without caution/warning lights at GET 000:51:00 (Schmitt: 'some spurious MASTER ALARM without caution and warning that seem to be associated with moving switches on panel 2 ... We've had about seven'). The specific MAIN A UNDERVOLT flicker was reported by Evans at 006:40:03; ground responded in ~15 s (1 turn) that they saw no glitch on MAIN A and floated a tentative accumulator-cycle correlation. IMPORTANT: this 15 s figure is the ground's real-time no-fault-found assessment, NOT a root-cause diagnosis. The alarms were never definitively diagnosed in-flight (CapCom at 001:57:39: 'we've searched all the data we can, and we cannot find anything wrong ... not able to tie in anything common'; by 073:07 still a 'witch hunt'). Per MR §15.1.1 the postflight cause was an intermittent short-to-ground in the main bus A undervoltage warning circuit / short to ground in panel 2 (postflight inspection of panel-2 wiring and the reset switch found no definitive contamination). Confidence medium because 'diagnosis' here is the immediate ground assessment, not the postflight root cause.

anomalies.symptom: cryogenic hydrogen tank pressure deadband narrowed, contaminated pressure switch
anomalies.notes: REAL Apollo 17 anomaly but GROUND/TELEMETRY-DETECTED, not crew-reported. Mission Report (EPS / cryogenic storage): 'the hydrogen tank 2 automatic pressure switch failed to operate properly after approximately 70 hours. After this time, pressure was manually controlled in hydrogen tanks 1 and 2.' A pressure switch not cycling the heaters within its deadband is seen on ground telemetry (cryo pressure/heater currents), and the fix (manual heater control) was ground-directed — the transcript shows Houston repeatedly commanding H2 heater/fan configurations throughout the flight (e.g., 034:55, 064:09, 071:xx). No crew air-to-ground fault report about an H2 pressure switch or narrowed deadband was located in the full transcript. crew_initiated=false is the correct, honest answer. (MR attributes it to the switch 'failing to operate properly'; the 'contaminated' descriptor in the prompt is not explicitly stated by MR for the H2 switch.)

anomalies.symptom: EMS accelerometer null-bias shift, 0.05g light illuminated erroneously
anomalies.exchange_quote: 303:06:10 CMP (Evans): 'Hey, Houston, let me doublecheck on this. The .05 G light was on, in EMS TEST 1, when I went to NORMAL. And it seems to me like that's normal but it may not be. Could we check on that for sure.'  303:06:10 CC: 'Okay, we're checking on that.'  303:08:25 CC (Parker): 'Okay, Ron, as you're going through the test, just a word on that EMS TEST 1. It is not normal for the zero - .05 G light to be on in ENTRY TEST mode 1. It is probably a result of that drifting accelerometer.'
anomalies.notes: CREW-REPORTED and confirmed real (Mission Report §15.1.5 'Entry Monitor System Accelerometer Bias Shift': null bias shifted from +0.01 to +0.66 ft/sec^2 before TEI, settling at +0.20; 'During step 1 of the system test prior to entry, the 0.05g light illuminated erroneously ... A large accelerometer null bias ... can account for the sensed 0.05-g level'). Two related crew reports: (a) at GET 300:36:08 Evans reported anomalous EMS numbers ('we've got a minus 29.2 on the DELTA-V test function of the EMS'; 'Not [happy] on the null bias check'), after which ground advised burning on NOUN 85s/burn time rather than EMS (300:59 'we concur ... not using EMS'). (b) The 0.05g-in-TEST-1 report quoted above: Evans queried Houston at 303:06:10 (he initially thought it normal), and after an interim 'we're checking' hold, CapCom diagnosed at 303:08:25, tying the erroneous 0.05g light to the drifting accelerometer — ~135 s, ~2 air-to-ground turns. Reinforced immediately after ('Again, it's probably the result of that drifting accelerometer'). Clean, quotable crew-report -> CapCom-diagnosis exchange.

anomalies.symptom: water-glycol temperature control valve failed to open properly
anomalies.notes: REAL Apollo 17 anomaly but GROUND/TELEMETRY-DETECTED, not crew-reported. Mission Report §15.1.10 ('Water/Glycol Temperature Control Valve Failed To Maintain The Evaporator Temperature'): 'During four early lunar orbit revolutions, the water/glycol temperature control valve (mixing valve) failed to open properly as the radiator outlet temperature decreased. The mixed coolant temperature momentarily fell as much as 4 deg F below the specification control band of 42-48 deg F during mixing startup. No corrective action was taken and initiation of mixing was proper during all subsequent lunar orbits.' This automatic mixing-valve behavior and the mixed-coolant/radiator-outlet temperatures are monitored on ground telemetry, and MR explicitly notes no crew action was taken. No matching crew air-to-ground fault report was found (the only crew glycol traffic concerns the SECONDARY glycol pump running 'ragged/oscillating' at GET ~109:15 — a different component — and routine evaporator activation). crew_initiated=false is the correct, honest answer.

anomalies.symptom: LM oxygen demand regulator A suit-loop leakage during EVA depressurization, switched to regulator B
anomalies.notes: REAL Apollo 17 LM anomaly but GROUND/TELEMETRY-DETECTED, not crew-reported. Mission Report §8.9 / §15.2.2: 'demand regulator A ... caused a rise in pressure in the suit loop while it was unmanned during preparation for the third extravehicular activity. Demand regulator A was placed in the closed position and the pressure rise stopped ... left closed for the remainder of the lunar module operations. Regulator A was leaking at a rate between 0.03 to 0.05 lb/hr and was probably caused by contamination between the ball-poppet and seat.' In the transcript this is the EVA-3-prep episode at GET ~163:35: Houston DIRECTED the action — CC 163:35:21 'Okay, Jack. We'd like you to close REG A, please'; LMP 163:35:45 'REG A is CLOSED'; then Cernan 163:36:29 'Say, Bob, what did you see in REG A?' — confirming ground caught it via telemetry, not the crew. Ground later (170:45, 171:45) instructed leaving REG A closed and using PRESS REG B ('switched to regulator B'). So crew_initiated=false. (A separate EARLIER episode at GET 148:31-150:46 WAS crew-flagged — Cernan 148:33:08 'Challenger has been holding at about 5.5 ever since we got in here ... just so we are not venting anything' — but that slow cabin-pressure creep was ground-investigated and BOTH demand regs were found good in-flight; it did not confirm a reg-A leak. The prompt's 'during EVA depressurization' is approximate: MR states it was the unmanned suit loop during EVA-3 preparation.)
